items.abstract: <jats:p>Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) and reinforcement learning (RL) have driven progress in GUI automation. However, most existing methods rely on static, one-shot visual inputs and passive perception, lacking the ability to adaptively determine when, whether, and how to observe the interface. We present GUI-Eyes, a reinforcement learning framework for active visual perception in GUI tasks. To acquire more informative observations, the agent learns to make strategic decisions on both whether and how to invoke visual tools, such as cropping or zooming, within a two-stage reasoning process. To support this behavior, we introduce a progressive perception strategy that decomposes the decision-making into coarse exploration and fine-grained grounding, coordinated by a two-level policy. In addition, we design a spatially continuous reward function tailored to tool usage, which integrates both location proximity and region overlap to provide dense supervision and alleviate the reward sparsity common in GUI environments. On the ScreenSpot-Pro benchmark, GUI-Eyes-3B achieves 44.8% grounding accuracy using only 3k labeled samples, significantly outperforming both supervised and RL-based baselines. These results highlight that tool-aware active perception, enabled by staged policy reasoning and fine-grained reward feedback, is critical for building robust and data-efficient GUI agents.</jats:p>
title: GUI-Eyes: Tool-Augmented Perception for Visual Grounding in GUI Agents

items.abstract: <jats:p>Self-supervised visual odometry (SSVO) enables camera motion estimation without ground-truth supervision by jointly learning depth and camera pose, making it suitable for large-scale autonomous driving expert systems where reliable ego-motion estimation supports real-time decision-making and robust navigation. However, existing SSVO methods often suffer from ambiguous depth estimation, limited receptive fields in pose networks, and insufficient utilization of global semantic context. To address these challenges, this paper proposes GLEVO, a SSVO framework that integrates visual foundation models (VFMs) into both depth estimation and pose prediction. Specifically, GLEVO adopts Depth Anything V2 for robust depth estimation and leverages frozen multi-level features from DINOv2 as global semantic priors. To effectively exploit these priors for pose estimation, two modules are introduced: (1) a global-to-local cross-attention module (GS-LGCA) that fuses shallow DINOv2 features with depth-derived geometric cues to enhance local geometric discriminability, and (2) a gated cross-frame fusion module (GCFF) that adaptively aggregates temporal information across consecutive frames for improved pose prediction. In addition, a lightweight pose refinement network further reduces residual pose errors by exploiting deep semantic features from real and warped frames. Extensive experiments on the KITTI Odometry, KITTI-360, and Oxford RobotCar datasets demonstrate that the proposed method achieves consistent and competitive performance compared with representative SSVO approaches. These results indicate that incorporating global semantic priors from visual foundation models can significantly improve the robustness and accuracy of self-supervised visual odometry. Code is available at https://github.com/Smezzdl1996/GLEVO.</jats:p>
title: GLEVO: Global-Context Guided Local Geometry Enhancement for Self-Supervised Visual Odometry in Autonomous Driving via a Foundation Model

items.abstract: <jats:p>Visual complexity has significant research value across various fields, influencing both first impressions and user experiences. In the context of human–computer interactions, studies on visual complexity in user interface design have evolved progressively alongside technological advancements, and the quantification of visual complexity has been demonstrated to be significant. However, existing research has primarily focused on web interfaces. In contrast, mobile interfaces have less maneuverable space and rely on finger interactions, necessitating more targeted studies. Additionally, while model research has gradually emerged in recent years, there are still issues regarding the influence weight of each visual element in the mobile interface that need to be addressed. This study employed a multiple linear regression analysis to develop a measurement model based on the visual elements used in mobile GUI design, addressing the weighting of each metric from the designer’s perspective. Different from other studies, this study focused on the independent visual elements of the mobile phone interface. This measurement model offers designers intuitive and quantitative reference metrics, enhancing the efficiency of design iterations. Furthermore, it lays the groundwork for the development of visual-complexity measurement tools.</jats:p>
title: A Measurement Model for Visual Complexity in HCI: Focusing on Visual Elements in Mobile GUI Design
